Long Island. On August 27, 1776, the first major engagement of the Revolutionary War saw British General William Howe crush an American force under George Washington near Brooklyn, New York. Also known as the Battle of Brooklyn, it was part of Howe's campaign to capture New York City and establish a base of operations. Washington had divided his army between Long Island and Manhattan. Howe outflanked the Long Island contingent with a large British force moving around their left. The Americans held a series of defensive lines but American militia broke and fled when the British appeared unexpectedly from their rear. Regular troops fought a delaying action, but the damage was done. About 1,000 American soldiers fell, and nearly 1,000 were captured. British casualties were relatively light, fewer than 400. Washington's skillful evacuation of 9,000 troops across the East River under cover of darkness and fog prevented total encirclement and destruction and preserved his army to continue the war. The defeat forced Washington to evacuate Manhattan and retreat across New Jersey, a period of acute strategic crisis for the Continental cause.
